scenes.heading: Caching & Sessions with Redis (go-redis)
scenes.narration: Let's see how Go services use Redis with go-redis to cache reads, hold sessions, and rate-limit callers.

scenes.heading: The foundation
items: Rich typed structures: strings, hashes, sets, sorted sets, lists
Every command takes a context for cancellation and timeouts
scenes.narration: The foundation is a single redis-dot-Client created once at startup. It's goroutine-safe and manages its own connection pool, so you never open a connection per request. Redis is more than a key-value blob store — it gives you typed structures like hashes for session objects and sorted sets for leaderboards. And every command takes a context, so cancellation and per-call timeouts flow through cleanly.

scenes.heading: The cache-aside pattern
steps: On a hit, return the cached value
On redis.Nil, it's a miss — read the database
scenes.narration: The workhorse read pattern is cache-aside. Your code checks Redis first; on a hit it returns immediately. On a miss, Get returns the sentinel redis-dot-Nil — which is a normal miss, not an error — so you fall back to the database, write the result back into Redis with a time-to-live, and return it. The database stays authoritative, and the cache is a disposable accelerator that can be empty at any moment.

scenes.heading: Cache-aside, done correctly
scenes.narration: This is cache-aside in code, and it gets the two classic bugs right. First, we compare against redis-dot-Nil to treat a missing key as a miss rather than five-hundred-ing on the first request. Second, the Set call passes a ten-minute time-to-live — without a real expiration the key would live forever and turn your cache into an unbounded memory leak.

scenes.text: Always set a TTL, treat redis.Nil as a miss, and protect hot keys from stampedes with SET NX locks and jittered TTLs.
scenes.narration: So: always attach a time-to-live, treat redis-dot-Nil as a normal miss, and put distributed rate limits in Redis with INCR plus EXPIRE. And when a hot key expires, protect the database from a stampede using a SET-N-X rebuild lock, jittered TTLs, and singleflight.
